title: US Measles Cases Jump by 426 in One Week to 5,838, the Largest Rise in Decades
excerpt: The CDC's latest tally is the first since the Pan American Health Organization declared measles endemic in the United States again, ending an elimination status held since 2000.
body:
• Confirmed US measles cases rose by 426 in one week to 5,838 as of November 19, the largest one-week jump in decades and the 15th straight week of a triple-digit increase, according to the CDC.
  • On November 17 the Pan American Health Organization determined that endemic measles transmission has been re-established in the United States, Bolivia and Mexico, ending the elimination status the US earned in 2000.
  • State health departments have reported 12 measles-associated deaths in 2026, eight of them in Pennsylvania; the CDC has acknowledged six while it develops a standard definition for measles deaths.
  • 96% of cases are in people who are unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown. Two doses of the MMR vaccine are 97% effective — check your family's records, and ask your doctor about an early dose for infants from 6 months if you live in or are visiting an outbreak area.

The United States recorded its largest one-week jump in measles cases in decades, with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reporting 426 new confirmed infections and a national total of 5,838 cases as of November 19. The tally, published November 20, is the CDC's first since the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) declared measles endemic in the country again, and it marks the 15th consecutive week in which the national total has risen by more than 100 cases.

Elimination status, held since 2000, is gone

PAHO determined on November 17 that endemic measles transmission had been re-established in the United States, Bolivia and Mexico after finding that the same strain had circulated continuously in each country for at least 12 months. The United States had held measles elimination status since 2000. The CDC's own measles data page now records that sustained spread lasting at least 12 months led to the loss of that status in 2026.

The 5,838 confirmed cases were reported across 47 jurisdictions, with a further 18 cases among international visitors to the United States. The CDC has recorded 43 new outbreaks in 2026, and 96% of confirmed cases are outbreak-associated. The year's hospitalization rate stands at 11%, the same as in 2025. Nearly six in 10 patients are children or teenagers, though the outbreak is shifting toward adults: people aged 20 and older account for 41% of cases this year, up from 29% in 2025.

"We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status."

— Robert F. Kennedy Jr., US Health and Human Services Secretary, in a post on X

Where the outbreak is hitting hardest

Pennsylvania remains the epicentre, with 1,631 cases reported by the state this year, including 97 new infections this week. The state reported its eighth measles-associated death on November 18; officials have said all eight were among unvaccinated people. Wisconsin's health department reported 181 new cases this week, bringing its 2026 total to 832, concentrated in what Jonathan Temte of the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health described as "very closed communities," including Amish and Old Order Mennonite communities. Minnesota's total rose to 203 with 43 new cases, and Indiana's reached 227, up 56 in a week.

Virginia reported its first measles death of 2026 on November 20 — a child aged 0 to 4 who had tested positive — bringing the number of deaths reported by states this year to 12. The CDC has acknowledged six deaths and says the number is subject to change while it works with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists on a standardized definition for measles deaths.

"It is tragic and unnecessary when people suffer or die from vaccine-preventable diseases. We know vaccines work. We have the science. What we need now is the leadership and commitment to use them."

— James McDonald, New York State Health Commissioner

Why coverage slipped — and what families should do

The CDC notes that MMR vaccination coverage among US kindergartners has fallen from 95.2% in the 2019–20 school year to 92.4% in 2025–26, below the 95% level needed for community immunity and leaving approximately 280,000 kindergartners without documented completion of the MMR series. Michael Osterholm of the University of Minnesota's Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy has warned that the country is nowhere near the peak of the outbreak.

For Indian families in the US, the practical steps are direct. Verify that every household member has two documented MMR doses — the CDC states that two doses are 97% effective at preventing infection — using the CDC's measles cases and outbreaks page to check whether your state is affected. Wisconsin and Pennsylvania health officials advise an early MMR dose for babies as young as 6 months who live in or will visit areas where measles is detected, which is worth raising with your pediatrician before holiday travel. A study published November 16 also found measles infected 112 pregnant women and 13 newborns over 21 months, and urged clinicians to give exposed unvaccinated pregnant patients immune globulin within six days of exposure.

What happens next

Regaining elimination status requires interrupting continuous transmission, a process health officials measure in months, not weeks. Mr. Kennedy attributed the loss of status to worldwide COVID-era disruptions to routine childhood vaccination and noted that Canada, Mexico, Spain and the United Kingdom have also lost elimination status. Until transmission breaks, the CDC will keep publishing weekly confirmed-case totals each Thursday, and state health departments remain the fastest source for local outbreak information.
